knownFor: Teacher of rhetoric who became priest and then bishop of Hippo in Roman North Africa. He wrote the Confessions and the City of God and taught that God's grace comes first, a teaching the Western churches carried on and divided over.
datesNote: Possidius says he lived seventy-six years, almost forty of them as priest or bishop. H. T. Weiskotten reckons his birth at 13 November 354 from Augustine's own words on his birthday. Prosper's chronicle, as Mommsen prints it, dates his death to 28 August 430. Weiskotten's note gives 391 both for his ordination as priest and for his consecration as bishop beside Valerius, and has him succeed Valerius in 396 or 397; the dominant modern reconstruction puts his becoming bishop at about 395 to 396. The Confessions are dated 397 to 400 in the Library's works list. The City of God was begun after Rome fell to the Goths, which Dods's note dates to 410
placeNote: Born at Tagaste in the African province; taught at Tagaste, Carthage, Rome and Milan; priest and bishop at Hippo Regius, in modern Algeria
role: Teacher of rhetoric; priest and bishop of Hippo; writer

keyWorks.title: Confessions
keyWorks.about: thirteen books addressed to God, which he says praise God and stir the human mind and heart toward him; books one to ten are about himself and the last three about Scripture. They tell the turn in the garden at Milan

keyWorks.title: City of God
keyWorks.about: twenty-two books begun after Rome fell to the Goths, when worshippers of the old gods blamed the Christians; it holds that two loves made two cities, love of self the earthly city and love of God the heavenly

keyWorks.title: On the Spirit and the Letter
keyWorks.about: against the Pelagians: free will and teaching are not enough, and God gives the Holy Spirit, who forms in a person a delight in and love of the good. Luther's editor dates it to 412

traces: Of the twenty-five canons of the council of Orange in 529, its editor Friedrich Maassen finds that nine and eleven to twenty-five repeat word for word sentences Prosper drew from Augustine's works, and that the rest follow passages of his writings very closely. The chapters were confirmed by Boniface II. B. B. Warfield calls the result a guarded and somewhat weakened Augustinianism.

In 1521 Luther told his opponent Emser he would teach him better than any teacher he had had, except Augustine, if Emser had read his On the Spirit and the Letter; on letter and spirit in Scripture, he says, none of the others will teach him aright.
Calvin says Augustine was for a time of another opinion but, as he came to know Scripture better, retracted it as false, and that he could build a whole volume out of Augustine's words alone.

Cornelius Jansen, bishop of Ypres, gave twenty years to a book called Augustinus on Augustine's teaching on grace. Urban VIII condemned the book by a bull of 6 March 1642, and in 1653 Innocent X condemned the Five Propositions.
Possidius added a list of his works so that readers could copy them from the library of the church of Hippo, and says no student could read them all.
remembered: Possidius says he left monasteries and the church's library, and that in his books the faithful may always find him living.
Prosper called him excellent in every way and says he kept defending the grace of Christ to the end.
Isidore of Seville wrote that he outdid the other writers he names in mind and learning, and wrote so much that no one could copy or even read it all.
Facundus of Hermiane, an African bishop writing to Justinian, called him the wisest and most famous teacher of the churches of Christ.
Philip Schaff says his anti-Pelagian works had a powerful influence on the Reformers of the sixteenth century and on the Jansenists of the seventeenth.

uncertain: Most of his life comes from two voices. His own Confessions were written about ten years after the garden in Milan, as a bishop praying to God. Possidius, his friend and fellow bishop for almost forty years, wrote his Life to honor him and was on the winning side of every quarrel he tells. Prosper was Augustine's defender. J. M. Neale wrote in sympathy with the Jansenists.
His parents' faith. Possidius calls them honorable Christian parents; Augustine says his father was only a catechumen, and that recently. The brief leaves his parents out.
The year he became bishop. Weiskotten's note says 391, the same year it gives for his ordination as priest. The dominant modern reconstruction is about 395 to 396.
How long he fought the Pelagians. Possidius says almost ten years; Prosper has him still answering Julian at his death. The two counts may measure different things, so the brief gives no number.

The dates of the Confessions and the City of God. No held ancient source gives a year for either. The Confessions are dated 397 to 400 in the Library's works list, and the year 410 for the fall of Rome is Dods's note.

Orange. That its canons drew on Augustine is the finding of the editors, Maassen and Warfield, not a statement of the council, which says its chapters came from the apostolic see. Warfield calls the result a weakened Augustinianism. The canons themselves were not read canon by canon here.

In the garden scene, Knoll's Latin text prints a voice from the divine house, from one manuscript, S; all the other manuscripts and earlier editors read the neighboring house, as Pilkington's English does. The rendering follows the neighboring house.
In Letter 93 the town he names as brought back by fear of the emperors' laws is his own town. The letter does not name it, so the brief says only his own town.
His anti-Pelagian treatises are held here in English only; their Latin was not found in the Library.
The date of birth rests on Weiskotten's note, which reckons it from Augustine's De beata vita; that work is not held here.

briefReferences: Possidius, Life of Augustine, ch. I, tr. H. T. Weiskotten: born at Tagaste; taught rhetoric at Carthage, then Rome, then Milan, where the emperor had his court; heard Ambrose preach; baptized at Easter. Ch. IV: the people seized him, in tears, to be made a priest. Ch. XVIII: African councils moved two bishops of Rome to condemn the Pelagians, and Honorius decreed they be condemned by his laws. Ch. XXVIII: the Vandals besiege Hippo. Ch. XXXI: seventy-six years; the church's library to be kept for future generations; the poet's lines at the end.
Augustine, Confessions IV.2.2, tr. J. G. Pilkington: he taught rhetoric and put to sale a loquacity by which to overcome.
Confessions VI.6.9: the speech in praise of the emperor with many lies in it, and the well-fed beggar, joking and glad, in a street of Milan.
Confessions VIII.12.28 to 30: the fig tree and the tears; the voice of a boy or girl from the house next door; Paul's letters opened at Romans 13:13-14; his mother's joy.

Augustine, Retractations II.1, and On the Predestination of the Saints 8, tr. Holmes and Wallis: his answer to Simplicianus, bishop of Milan, on Romans 9, at the start of his time as bishop; God's grace won.

Augustine, Letter 93 to Vincentius, about 408, 5.17 and 2.5: at first he held that no one should be forced into the church; his own town brought back by fear of the emperors' laws; compel them to come in.
Augustine, Retractations II.43, as given in Dods's City of God: Rome sacked by the Goths under Alaric, the pagans blaming the Christian religion. City of God XIV.28: two loves made two cities.
Augustine, On the Spirit and the Letter 5: free will and teaching are not enough; the Holy Spirit forms in a person a love of the good.

Friedrich Maassen, ed., Council of Orange (529), in Concilia aevi Merovingici: canons drawn from Augustine's writings and from Prosper's Sentences. B. B. Warfield, introduction to the anti-Pelagian writings: the second synod of Orange.

Luther, Answer to Emser (1521): no teacher but Augustine, in On the Spirit and the Letter, would teach him rightly. Calvin, Institutes III.22.8: a whole volume out of Augustine's words alone. J. M. Neale, History of the So-called Jansenist Church of Holland: Jansen's Augustinus, condemned by Urban VIII in 1642.

World census, the Latin Pastoral Congregations: his tradition. World census, Donatism and Pelagianism: the Donatist church, a rival African church for a century, and Pelagius's teaching that God had given human nature the power to do good.

quotationOriginals.modern: And look, I hear a voice from the house next door, singing and repeating it again and again, like a boy's or a girl's voice, I do not know which: 'Take it and read, take it and read.'
quotationOriginals.printed: et ecce audio uocem de diuina domo cum cantu dicentis et crebro repetentis quasi pueri an puellae, nescio: „tolle lege, tolle lege“.
quotationOriginals.work: Augustine, Confessions VIII.12.29, Latin, ed. Knoll, CSEL 33
quotationOriginals.uncertain: Knoll prints diuina (divine) from one manuscript, S; the apparatus at line 13486 gives uicina (neighboring) for all the others and earlier editors. The rendering follows uicina, as Pilkington's English does.

quotationOriginals.modern: In answering this question, I worked hard for the free choice of the human will. But God's grace won. I could only come to see that the apostle spoke the plainest truth: 'Who sets you apart? What do you have that you did not receive?'
quotationOriginals.printed: in cuius quaestionis solutione laboratum est quidem pro libero arbitrio uoluntatis humanae, sed uicit dei gratia, nec nisi ad illud potuit perueniri, ut liquidissima ueritate dixisse intellegatur apostolus: quis enim te discernit? quid autem habes, quod non accepisti?
